title: How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

It’s a time-tested tradition: Presidents looking to reassert authority and escape political gloom head overseas for a global pick-me-up.

Ever since 1982, when Ronald Reagan traded a recession, 11% unemployment and Democrats’ 26-seat pickup for a five-day swing through Latin America, Air Force One has been leaving political upheaval behind in its contrail.

President Donald Trump will attempt to follow suit this week with a long-planned trip through Asia, punctuated Thursday by an unprecedented three-waymeeting with his authoritarian counterparts from China and Russia— a splashy show of geopolitical theater alongside men whose power in their own countries goes mostly unchallenged.

Asked Monday morning if he felt the midterm losses could diminish his influence abroad, Trump replied: “No,” saying he wasn’t the one on the ballot and that voters were “unhappy” with Congress.

But comparisons between powerful leaders abroad and a newly constrained US leader may be unavoidable.

The sharp rebuke Trump faced from voters this month was quickly clocked by his foreign counterparts, all watching closely for signs of fading political capital and early-onset lame-duck status. He’ll be joined on the trip by Elon Musk, whose$445 million in political spendingfailed to deliver Republican majorities.

“Foreign policy and presidential trips are something only the president can do. There is pomp and circumstance. There’s a focus on it,” said Edgard Kagan, a former US ambassador to Malaysia who is now senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington. “This is a way in which you start changing the narrative, and remind people that, you know, the president is still the president.”

It’s not the only complication on Trump’s plate. The scandal involving Jensen Huang’s high-powered AI chips andaffair with an alleged Chinese spywill loom over the US president’s visit to Shenzhen, the gleaming hub of China’s tech industry, even though Trump’s aides insist it wouldn’t dominate the journey.

Trump said on Monday that he “might” bring upthe spying matterwith Chinese leader Xi Jinping, with whom he will meet for the fourth time in just over a year, though American officials previously told CNN they didn’t expect him start those conversations. Officials said they also did not expect the two men to discuss the newly revived debate inside the administration over how to furtherrestrict high-powered chips from going to China.

“It’s probably not something we’re going to read the Chinese in on at the moment,” one senior US official said.

Never particularly enthusiastic about grueling trips through far-flung time zones, Trump departs for the Philippines Monday after shaking up his West Wing leadership and facing calls even from some allies to fire members of his Cabinet, including the secretaries of Commerce and Defense. Anair travel meltdownbefore he left — which Trump did not address publicly for days — also raised new questions about his mindset and focus heading into the trip.

At two leaders summits — the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) in Shenzhen — Trump will look to counter the narrative of his declining power by announcing new commercial deals and asserting American presence in a region that for decades has suffered from Washington’s inattention.

Like his most recent predecessors, Trump has found the “pivot to Asia” an elusive concept. His second term became bogged down by a war in the Middle East, the same region that kept George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden from fully turning American foreign policy toward the Pacific.

Trump has spent the past year working to cultivate deeper ties with Xi. And he’s been seeking new trade deals, with plans to sign an agreement with Thailand this week, White House officials said.

Yet the Iran war, along with Trump’s so-farfutile efforts to end the war in Ukraine, continue to dominate his foreign policy agenda. Both are likely to hang over his talks this week in Asia, where fuel prices have spiked due to the conflicts. He declined to answer Monday whether he would ask Xi to stop buying Iranian oil, saying, “I’ll ask them what I want to ask them.”

And Democrats’ stateside victories will lead to questions of just how much Trump has left to offer. His two signature foreign policy initiatives — global tariffs and the Iran war — led to price increases that propelled voter anger toward him and Republicans. Democrats have vowed to limit his authorities on both, challenging the long-held adage that a president has a freer hand on foreign matters.

A foreign trip has long been a way to drive home that point while also escaping Washington as the opposition prepares to assume power. Michael Deaver, an image-maker to Reagan, is credited with inventing the tactic when he arranged the Latin America trip in 1982.

Nearly every president since then has replicated the idea. Bill Clinton made a trip to the Philippines in November 1994 after Republicans swept control of Congress for the first time in decades. George W. Bush was in Vietnam a few weeks after the GOP lost Congress in 2006. Barack Obama headed to Asia in 2010 and 2014 after midterm routs. And Trump himself made a somewhat desultory visit to France in 2017 after the GOP lost its majority in the House.

“I’ve been with presidents immediately after midterm, both wins and losses, and it’s always important,” Kagan said. “It’s something that reminds the nation, it reminds foreign observers, that this is very much the president’s bailiwick.”

For Trump, that means appearing in a joint setting with powerful men to discuss the world’s affairs. For some, the meeting between Trump, Xi and Russian leader Vladimir Putin carries unpleasant echoes of the 1945 conference in the Crimean resort of Yalta, where Stalin, Churchill and an extremely ill Franklin D. Roosevelt carved up the postwar world into western and eastern spheres of influence.

Putin originally proposed the three-party summit as a venue to discuss the Ukraine war, where fraught issues of borders and sovereignty loom over nascent peace talks. Trump said Monday he intends to discuss the war in Ukraine with his Russian and Chinese counterparts, despite US officials suggesting last week the topic wouldn’t be on the table, as it wouldn’t be “appropriate” since separate peace discussions are underway, led by Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff.

Trump’s aides insisted that he hopes to use the meeting to open discussions on nuclear weapons with two leaders he’s worked hard to cultivate. The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia — which each have an estimated 5,000 warheads — expired in February. China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its arsenal to more than 600 warheads but shows little interest in joining a pact.

A US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said expectations were low for a major breakthrough, describing the talks instead as a starting point.

“It’s time for China to sort of step up to the adult table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the official said.

Xi had initially appeared skeptical of hosting the meeting, officials said, concerned it could overshadow the APEC summit and his attempts to showcase a rising China. But on Monday China’s foreign ministry billed it as meeting of “groundbreaking significance,” with spokesperson Mao Ning saying “such efforts would will help stabilize the global situation.”

Trump, who sometimes says he envies authoritarians who rule as they wish, signed on quickly.
